title: The Rise and Fall of 'The Resistance'
content:
To unlock more of my reporting on how the internet is reshaping politics, business, media, and culture, and to read my deep dives into emerging online spaces and internet trends, become a paid subscriber today!

I cannot produce this newsletter without your financial support. Your money goes directly towards reporting costs.

In January I was back in Washington D.C. to cover the inauguration. Thousands of Trump supporters waited hours in sub freezing temperatures to catch a glimpse of the president at a rally held at the Capital Arena. Just minutes away, Trump was sworn in as the 47th president in the Capitol Rotunda. On the day of the inauguration,

I walked from the Capitol to the arena, up Pennsylvania, past the Waldorf Astoria (formerly the Trump hotel), towards the White House. I did not witness a single protest. It was cold, but Trump supporters cheered in the streets, drank, ate, and waltzed around in the deluge of merch available at outdoor kiosks.

Eight years ago, in 2017, the picture could not have been more different. Just hours after Trump was sworn in, widespread protests erupted across D.C. and other cities. Thousands of people took to the streets. More than 200 demonstrators were arrested during confrontations that resulted in property damage and clashes with law enforcement into the wee hours of the morning.

The next day, over half a million people swarmed the streets of D.C. for the Women’s March, one of the largest single-day protests in U.S. history. Every single week, for months, there were marches and mass protests with thousands of people. There was the science march, the tax march, the march for truth, a march to call for Trump's impeachment, and dozens more.

The protests underlied what ultimately became known as "the resistance", a movement that consisted of Hillary-supporting liberals, disaffected conservatives who opposed Trump's agenda, and a smattering of progressive activists, all of whom banded together to oppose Trump's policies and actions. The movement garnered widespread support on social media platforms though hashtags like #Resist and #TheResistance, which trended on Twitter and Instagram throughout 2017.

The resistance movement was fed by a steady stream of resistance media. Traditional news organizations like CNN and The Washington Post attempted to ride the resistance wave. In February 2017, just a month after Trump took power, The Washington Post changed its slogan to "Democracy Dies in Darkness."

Just days after Trump's inauguration, a bunch of Twitter users who ostensibly worked in the federal government set up anonymous Twitter accounts and grew huge followings from allegedly "resisting" Trumpism from the inside. These rogue resistance accounts included @RogueNOAA (for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration), @RogueNASA (for the space agency) and @alt_fda for the Food and Drug Administration.An account called AltEPA with more than 150,000 followers, claimed that it would be offering data that might be suppressed by the Environmental Protection Agency under Trump. "He can take our official Twitter but he'll never take our FREEDOM," the account posted. "UNOFFICIALLY resisting." The posts gained traction with hashtags like #ResistTrump.

Another account known as "Angry Staffer", claimed to be a resistance mole within the White House. It posted liberal bait like, "Given what I'm seeing here, I'm left with one option to save this nation. I'm going to start leaking EVERYTHING. Dm me if you're media." Of course, the leaks never came.

An entire ecosystem of alternative media and anti-Trump influencers quickly arose to feed the hunger for 24/7 anti-Trump news. The online resistance boom birthed a slew of podcasts, newsletters, and Twitter personalities who stoked liberal conspiracism about Russiagate and an impending impeachment. In their minds, Robert Muller was always one step away from putting Trump behind bars.

There was Muller, She Wrote, a once anonymous account that posted detailed commentary on Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the election. There were also figures like Brooklyn Dad Defiant, a centrist lib poster who fed anti-Trump conspiracies to his liberal followers throughout Trump' first term. Brooklyn Dad Defiant, used his fame to publish a series of anti-Trump childrens book like one called, "The Liddle'est President."

Back then, Democratic politicians were outspoken about the danger they claimed Trump posed. Rep. Maxine Waters called Trump's advisors "scumbags" and stated that the White House "is now the White Supremacists' House." Rep. Al Green called for Trump's impeachment on the house floor.

The resistance helped spur social movements that arose throughout Trump's first presidency. There was the effort to abolish ICE and reform immigration, #MeToo, which sought to draw attention to misogynistic hate and abuse of women, the Black Lives Matter movement, which peaked in 2020 following the murder of George Floyd.

Support for Bernie Sanders surged in the primaries, and many young people felt hopeful that we might be moving toward a more progressive future. When the Covid pandemic hit, liberals fought for public health measures and clanged pots and pans outside their windows to support healthcare workers, and protected the vulnerable.

Five years later, the resistance is dead.

Not only did liberals face a definitive electoral loss to Trump this time around, there is no widespread and cohesive coalition fighting Trump's actions and policies. Trumpism has completely subsumed the Republican establishment, right wing reactionary ideology is becoming culturally dominant, and many liberals (including many in congress) are fully willing to hop on board with Trump's agenda.

"Democrats do not seem as anguished or animated by this Trump Restoration as they were by his ascension; neither are they howling about their own party’s future," the journalist Ross Barkan recently wrote in The New York Times. "The left — looking up after eight years of resisting Trump and finding that in fact, he has expanded his vote share in each general election — is recalibrating… Border policies that were decried as fascistic in Trump’s first term are gradually being embraced, or at least no longer resisted. The old discourse around the 'normalization' of Trump is dead; businesses that once stood at a remove from Trump giddily treat him as an ordinary president now."

The dismantling of the resistance didn't happen overnight. Cracks in the resistance coalition began to show as early as the 2020 primaries, when Democratic leaders rallied around Biden in order to crowd out the more progressive candidate, Bernie Sanders. Some on the left felt betrayed, but many held out hope that Biden might enact some of the more progressive changes they wanted to see.

Unfortunately, after gaining office, the Biden administration worked to alienate many core progressive constituencies. Biden immediately responded to the Black Lives Matter movement, by showering the cops with even more funding. This resulted in the police murdering even more innocent civilians with impunity. 2023 was the deadliest year ever for civilians killed by police, with at least 1,232 people killed by law enforcement, according to the non profit Mapping Police Violence. Black Americans were disproportionately affected, being 2.9 times more likely to be killed by police than white Americans.

Biden also reneged on his campaign promises to expand public health measures and protect disabled people and the broader public from mass death and disability from Covid. Instead of instituting long term public health protections, he dismantled our public health infrastructure, mandated forced infection by lifting all airborne disease mitigations, forcing people back to work, and enacting policies on Covid that were further to the right of Trump in 2020— all while prematurely declaring the pandemic "over" because companies like Delta airlines asked him to. (The Covid pandemic is still raging according to the World Health Organization, which has never declared it over).

Biden also failed to fulfill promises he made to young people related to climate change and student debt. When massive Gen Z influencers who helped get him elected attempted to hold the administration accountable on issues like Covid and Gaza, Biden responded by blacklisting those very influencers from the White House. His administration cracked down hard on protesters and worked to dismantle Americans' free speech and civil liberties through pushing for laws like the TikTok ban and criminal charges against student protesters fighting against his administration's support of the genocide in Gaza.

"Over the past few years we've seen two waves of some of the biggest protests and sustained actions in this country since the 1960s, with BLM and what has been happening over the past year and a half with Gaza," said Karl Folk, a researcher on political extremism. "The reaction from Democrats to both of those things-- from party leaders and higher income older folks in the Democratic coalition down-- has been very different than it was when protests were happening in 2017 and 2018."

Folk said that centrist liberals in Biden's coalition banding together to squash more progressive movements led to average people feeling disenchanted and hopeless. "It showed people that you can just ignore these big, massive protests and not pay any political price for it," he said. "The resistance died a death by 1,000 cuts."

The journalist Talia Jane echoed this analysis on X, noting that, "the reason protests aren’t having the impact they used to have is that those with power simply stopped caring about the social/shame impact of their actions."

People feel like no matter what they do, their voices will simply be ignored by people in power. They witnessed things like RICO charges being levied at protesters fighting against "cop city" in Atlanta, or young students at Columbia university facing federal charges for peaceful protests, all under Democratic leadership. Last year, organizers told me that taking to the streets felt risky in a way that it didn't just five years prior, before Biden was elected.

The social media landscape has also radically changed since Trump's first presidency. While it was easy to amass millions of impressions by tweeting Cofeve jokes about the cheeto in chief back in 2018, resistance figures now struggle to attract an audience outside a dwindling base who haven't evolved with the culture.

Back in 2017, algorithmic feeds were nascent, and social media platforms had yet to substantially crack down on progressive activism. Social movements could gain traction primarily through apps like Twitter, (now controlled by a far right billionaire), and TikTok, (banned by Biden and has since begun catering to Trump in hopes that he will reverse the ban). Instagram too, has shifted to the right, with Zuckberberg encouraging misogynistic and anti-LGBTQ hate speech, while still cracking down on accounts that post progressive speech like advocating for a free Palestine.

Many centrist Biden and Kamala-supporting liberals have also adopted the exact same strain of conspiracism that they once criticized Trump supporters for espousing. I wrote an article last year about the rise of "BlueAnon" and how the communal warping of reality is spreading far beyond the right. Democrats are increasingly likely to distrust the mainstream media and believe lies like the 2024 election was stolen and a secret "deep state" mafia is controlling things.

One Economist poll found that only 52% of Harris supporters said that they believe Trump “legitimately” won the 2024 election. Sure, liberals aren't storming the Capitol, but it's a lot harder to criticize MAGA supporters for living in an alternate reality, when you now believe the exact same thing about your own preferred candidate.

Researchers who study extremism have said that this centrist liberal strand of conspiratorial thinking arises when people are unwilling to accept developments that challenge their worldview. It's also exacerbated by shifts in media. The entire internet has evolved over recent years, and older generations like Boomers and Gen Xers are struggling to navigate this complex and fast-moving media climate.

While a certain subset of anti-Trump resistance influencers are still online crowing about Trump like it's 2018, many have realized that promoting that sort of liberalism under the current cultural climate is simply not as profitable as it once was. Trump won the popular vote, their conspiracies aren't panning out, so might as well hop on board the winning team.

You see this with figures like Lindy Li, a quintessential resistance influencer. Lindy Li is a Millennial political commentator who amassed hundreds of thousands of followers by being a shill for the Democratic party in the late 2010s. She grew an intense and loyal fandom of resistance liberals throughout Trump's first term by posting a non-stop stream of anti Trump news and messaging. When Biden was elected, she was relentless in her support of him. She backed Biden until the moment he was forced to drop out, and then became an ardent supporter of Kamala Harris.

Li's social media feed was overrun with adoring posts featuring herself at events with the president, vice president, and other top Democratic elected officials like Nancy Pelosi. “There will never be another like her,” she said of Pelosi. She also was part of the Pennsylvania delegation at the Democratic National Convention this summer. Li called Trump "serial rapist" on national television and lambasted the Republican Party. She attended all the White House influencer events and panels, and dutifully worked in lock step with the Biden administration to destory any cohesive resistance efforts from the progressive left.

But after the Democrats lost this time around, Li pivoted. She started bashing Kamala's campaign and began to engage more actively with pro-Trump media. She lauded the momentum of Trump's transition, and by January 2025, Li was actively fundraising for Republican candidates and even Trump himself.

She referred to Pete Hegseth, Trump's candidate for secretary of defense, who had a long list of allegations of sexual assault, alcohol abuse, and corruption, as “a pretty good guy.” Li now claims that she “has been a conservative all her life,” that Democrats are to blame for failing to secure the southern border, that there will be a “new era of prosperity” under Donald Trump, and that “The markets and consumer confidence have been booming under Pres. Trump. Americans are loving this transition.”

Li's evolution makes sense when you consider that many influencers who spent the years 2017 to 2020 pushing resistance content, are now refashioning themselves as conservatives, as brands and big money interests seek to make inroads with the conservative movement.

Then there's the fact that when you scratch just below the surface, many of the resistance's most ardent and prominent supporters during Trump's first term, especially white, upper middle class Gen X women and boomers, weren't actually that liberal when it came down to it.

"The entirety of the resistance movement was a conservative movement that was intended to sell you hope for cash," said Folk, the extremism researcher.

While many white people, especially white women, were happy to march in the streets when they thought Trump's policies might directly affect them, they ultimately had no solidarity with poor people or the working class. Once they realized they weren't going to be as affected by the worst of Trump's policies, and once Trumpism became more normalized in their social circles, they went back to brunch.

Many liberals who made up the resistance from 2016 to 2020, seemed to primarily dislike Trump because of his crass, sexist language and disdain for political norms. But many of those same liberals ultimately didn't have problems with many of Trump's policies, as long as someone from their blue team was enacting them. They happily embraced Trump's far right agenda surrounding immigration, Covid, and funding Israel's genocide— when Biden carried it out. The resistance movement itself was mostly full of reactionary conservatives.

You can see this very clearly when you dig into the pasts of many of the resistance's most well known influencers.

Ron Filipowski, one of the big resistance voices online, worked for Ron DeSantis until 2020. Muller She Wrote, another big resistance influencer, was a failed stand-up comic who used slurs on stage. Before Brooklyn Dad Defiant pivoted his account into a resistance page, he was pushing “defiance” of court-ordered child support and spouting reactionary rhetoric that the court system is biased against men. The resistance influencer Jack Hopkins is a rebranded pseudonym for a men’s rights activist who was extremely deep into some of the most severely misogynistic and anti woman spaces on the internet in the 2000s. And the list goes on. The defining feature among some of the most well known resistance figures is that they're fundamentally conservative.

Just look at The Bulwark, the single biggest "resistance media" outlet still standing. It’s published by Tim Miller, the former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, who served as communications director for Jeb Bush's 2016 presidential campaign. Sarah Longwell, another co-founder of The Bulwark, is a former Republican lobbyist who says she believes the best form of government is "principled conservatism."

The Bulwark's other big name writer is Bill Kristol, a neoconservative commentator who founded the right wing magazine The Weekly Standard, and who worked in the Regan and Bush administrations. Kristol played a leading role in the defeat of the Clinton health care plan and advocated for the Iraq war. Kristol is also a member of the board of trustees for the Manhattan Institute, the extreme far right think tank that literally birthed the entire movement to dismantle DEI.

When these are the biggest voices in the movement to ostensibly resist facism, it's easy to see why efforts have failed. Folk told me, "I can walk through almost any of these accounts with receipts showing that they are in fact, deeply conservative, and in some cases far right."

Many resistance figures came to understand that it was almost impossible to make money in an already saturated environment on the right in the late 2010s, so they decided to court and take money from liberals. Now that the culture has swung away from liberalism and Trump won the popular vote, these conservative voices no longer need to pretend to provide a counter to conservatism. They can do what Biden ultimately did, which is provide a gradual and comforting off ramp for many liberals to accept right wing extremism.

The left wing of the party has been effectively hollowed out and threatened into submission. And many leftists have even come around to supporting Trump's reactionary policies. Major leftist organizations, for instance, are unwilling to show even the most basic solidarity with disabled people by advocating for public health protections or fighting for the working class.

Some people in a delusional alternate reality, might imagine that the mainstream media would keep these fundamentally reactionary influencers in check, but that arm of the resistance has been hollowed out too.

Last summer, The Washington Post ousted their first female editor in chief and replaced senior staff with former Rupert Murdoch staffers. After Trump was elected again, they changed their slogan from the resistance-era Democracy Dies in Darkness, to "Riveting Storytelling for All of America." Leaders at the company spoke out about seeking to court a more conservative audience. CNN, once an anti-Trump stronghold, is making aggressive efforts to incorporate conservative perspectives into its programming. A prominent example is the inclusion of Scott Jennings, a conservative commentator known for articulating the viewpoints of "Red America."

The New York Times has also taken steps to broaden its editorial scope by engaging with conservative voices. Meanwhile, The Los Angeles Times has explored avenues to cater to right wing audiences more directly. LA Times owner Patrick Soon-Shiong is even considering launching a MAGA-friendly digital news outlet featuring Candace Owens, called LAT Next.

While the mainstream media spent Trump's first term pearl clutching over norms, they have now all basically accepted that they will treat him like any other president, and readers and viewers should too. On top of the mainstream media and tech world's rightward shift, conservatives have also built a massive right wing media infrastructure of social platforms catered specifically toward pushing pro-Trump and reactionary messages. Rumble, Truth Social, and myriad other right wing social media apps pump out conservative messaging and erode support for liberalism across the internet.

The decline of the "resistance" movement does offer one critical lesson: that superficial opposition, led by establishment figures and former Republican operatives, was never poised to effect genuine liberation from right-wing extremism. This performative dissent always lacked the structural depth and grassroots foundation necessary for substantive change.

The fact that the "resistance" relied so heavily on individuals deeply entrenched in the existing political framework meant that it was always doomed to fail. Figures like Liz Cheney, despite their vocal opposition to certain Trump policies, will always fundamentally uphold conservative agendas that conflict with progressive ideals. Making these types of people, along with a slew of social media opportunists, the face of the political movement against right-wing extremism was always absurd. Because when you dig right down, their foundational beliefs ultimately align with the very candidate that they're purporting to resist.

The commodification of dissent within the "resistance" movement also undermined its credibility. These resistance influencers commercialized their activism, transforming "resistance" into a lucrative enterprise devoid of genuine commitment to change. This commercialization not only diluted the movement's message but also alienated people seeking real change instead of performative online posturing.

To effectively counter right-wing extremism, we need to cultivate a broad-based movement rooted in class solidarity. This type of approach must go beyond archaic partisan divides and must focus on the shared economic struggles that unite all working and poor people in America.

It requires admitting that people are struggling to make ends meet, they can't get access to healthcare, and many are being exploited by their jobs. These are all issues that establishment Democrats and members of the "resistance" shamed progressives for bringing up throughout Biden's presidency and Kamala's campaign. I do think that as Trump fails to deliver on his promises there is room for some sort of political alternative to emerge. But it should not be one that comes from the establishment.

Just look at the recent reaction to Luigi Mangione. There is a collective frustration and anger Americans are feeling that transcends traditional political affiliations, and right now the far right are the only ones even acknowledging that anger. An anger that the liberal "resistance" completely failed to address. Real change will require grassroots organizing, community engagement, and rooting out establishment figures whose goals are not aligned with working people.

"Resistance" shouldn't be a media brand or a personality cult. Reactionary politics can’t be countered by smug Tweets, hashtags, cable news talking points, or Ruth Bader Ginsberg merch. Ultimately the death of the resistance presents an opportunity to reconstruct opposition to right wing extremism on a more solid foundation. It gives the next generation of "resistance" the opportunity to fight for actual systemic change. This evolution is crucial if we want to create a political system that truly serves everyone's needs, not just the needs of the rich establishment.
